More precisely, if R is a CommRing and A is a Ring and an R-algebra, then of
course A is an R-module, and this is what Algebra.toModule says. However,
if Mathlib.Algebra.Lie.Basic is imported, then I claim that Algebra.toModule will never
fire. Here's my argument (which needs checking).

The reason is this. Algebra.toModule and LieAlgebra.toModule both have
discrimination tree Module _ _ _ _, and currently the randomness of import order
seems to ensure that Algebra.toModule is defined first (perhaps because A comes
before L in the alphabet) and hence is tried last.

However if Algebra.toModule will succeed (i.e. if Ring A and Algebra R A exist)
then LieAlgebra.toModule will also succeed, because
LieRing.ofAssociativeRing [Ring A] : LieRing A and
LieAlgebra.ofAssociativeAlgebra [CommRing R] [Ring A] [Algebra R A] : LieAlgebra R A are all the ingredients it needs.

I think this explains (at least partially) why one sees so much Lie stuff in algebra traces.
How badly would it affect Lie theory if these docs#LieRing.ofAssociativeRing and co would be scoped to some Lie namespace?
Or should we decrease their prio?

My guess is that scoping should be fine but perhaps one has to think about exactly which namespace to scope them to. I think that this used to be a bigger problem but now we have manually squeezed out many of the spurious Lie algebra imports in algebra (they were there probably precisely because of this phenomenon), but I'll need to import them for automorphic forms (because part of the definition uses Lie algebras).

@Sébastien Gouëzel would decreasing their prio contradict your ideas about increasing prio of projections from preferred parents? Module is the preferred (in fact only) parent of LieAlgebra.

I don't want to increase prio of projections from preferred parents. I would like to

  • make sure that specific instances get prio 2000 at instance construction (this requires a change in core)
  • then choose a small number of instances, which are the spine of our algebra construction and that we would like to try early on, and increase the priority of these to 1500, say.

If we consider that Algebra.toModule is part of these preferred things that should be tried early on, we could increase its prio to 1500 (but not before the core change). But I'd say this is the kind of change that should not be done lightly, i.e., we should benchmark carefully each such change.

Decreasing the prio of LieAlgebra.toModule to 900 also looks perfectly reasonable to me. And that can be done today.
I think this has been discussed before, but I don’t see why LieRing.ofAssociativeRing should be an instance instead of a def.
I think because we often want to treat End(V) as both a ring and a lie algebra. Files doing that could locally instancify that decl. Or we scope it.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

  • make sure that specific instances get prio 2000 at instance construction (this requires a change in core)

Can someone with meta-programming skills hack together an experimental instance-keyword elaborator that does this prio 2000 change?

So that we can then experiment with

  • then choose a small number of instances, which are the spine of our algebra construction and that we would like to try early on, and increase the priority of these to 1500, say.

on top of it?

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

I don't want to increase prio of projections from preferred parents. I would like to

  • make sure that specific instances get prio 2000 at instance construction (this requires a change in core)

What do we mean by "specific instances", exactly? The ones whose discrimination tree key is not just Class _ _ ... _? Or is there something else about them? Because IIRC the algorithm already prefers more precise keys over less precise ones.
Here #mathlib4 > Definition of `Ring` @ 💬 is where Sébastien explains his idea more clearly.

Anne Baanen said:

What do we mean by "specific instances", exactly? The ones whose discrimination tree key is not just Class _ _ ... _?

Yes, exactly these. Indeed they are preferred over less specific instance, but only when they have the same priority, so if we increase the priority of a less specific instance from 1000 to 1500, say, then it will be tried beore all the specific instances, which is bad.
Got it, thanks! I could try building a test macro that does this, maybe already doing this for just Mathlib would be a good test case.
I expect it won't make a difference in Mathlib in its current state, but it would make it possible to try some tweakings that are impossible today.
Here's a basic but somewhat limited implementation (see TODOs): #40114
Any instance downstream of Mathlib.Init should get a priority bump if it is more specific. I don't expect any build failures, but we'll need to see since it is a slight bit hacky.
It looks like there is a big performance issue here -- the build has been going on for 1h40 and it's not done yet, it's at less than 6000 files.
I was about to say the same. Also we've been getting build failures (mostly timeouts or instances not being found?)
Do you think it's an issue with your extension (which would take a lot of time) or a genuine problem coming from the change of priorities?

My guess is it's an issue with the extension, and not with the priority change: in #40120 I try a version where the 2000 is replaced by 1000 (so the priorities should be the original ones) and still it takes forever to build.

Ah hmm, I use the same mechanism as whatsnew in to figure out which instances got added: iterate over environments and take their difference. I figured that would be fast enough. But maybe there's a more efficient way to do it?
Can you just replace instance directly?

We'd also want this for @[instance] def and class ... extends ... though. And I don't know if there's a good way to actually override the elaborator for instance specifically, since this all goes through the elabDeclaration machinery

I'm not sure it's important for @[instance] def and class extends, because the first one is very rare in Mathlib, and the second one most often doesn't generate specific instances. I'd say what we need is just a hacky implementation to do our optimization tests, not something rock solid.

Shouldn't we decrease the priority of non-specific instances to 100?

The library note "lower instance priority" said:

Certain instances always apply during type-class resolution. For example, the instance
AddCommGroup.toAddGroup {α} [AddCommGroup α] : AddGroup α applies to all type-class
resolution problems of the form AddGroup _, and type-class inference will then do an
exhaustive search to find a commutative group. (...)

Therefore, if we create an instance that always applies, we set the priority of these instances to
100 (or something similar, which is below the default value of 1000).
@Yuyang Zhao my impression is that Sébastien Gouëzel wants to automate a large chunk of those cases, albeit with different priority numbers.

Yes. The lower priority note made sense in Lean 3, but it's not as much needed in Lean 4 as there is the clever choice between specific and non-specific instances when they have the same priority. The outcome is that we are not any more adjusting the priorities by hand like that in the library, and we should probably delete the note.
Did we already delete the lowered priorities that occur where the note is applied?
I guess if we do and things get worse, we should replace the note with some remark about how this used to be principled and now is mysterious

I think most of the manual priority settings currently follow these library notes, so I feel lowering the priority is more appropriate in terms of the priority numbers. If we want to change this, it would be best to first confirm that we can revisit most of the corresponding priority adjustments in the library.

The priorities we're currently using include 50, 70, 100, 200, 900, etc. AFAIK we haven't done any major priority adjustments yet, and some of the manual settings still follow these library notes. Also, in lean3 we had extends_priority with a default of 100. So I think it's worth considering how to make use of the existing priority settings.

Scott Carnahan said:

I think this has been discussed before, but I don’t see why LieRing.ofAssociativeRing should be an instance instead of a def.

I agree with this: it should be demoted to adef. As I've written elsewhere, there are lots of reasons for this but the most compelling is that there are situations like general Poisson algebras where one wants both products docs#Mul and docs#Bracket (not necessarily satisfying the commutator relation).

I did once try to the demotion maybe two years ago but it was a bit painful. Possibly Claude could do it now!
#40306 tries this: mathlib builds; let's see if it's worth it. (The implementation is of prototypical quality; adopting this into something refined is welcome!)

Thanks for #40306. I'll record here that in an ideal world we'd go in further and use docs#LieRing.ofAssociativeRing only in proofs but not in statements.

The design I have in mind is that we'd introduce a new typeclass:

class IsLieCommutator (A : Type*) [Mul A] [Sub A] [Bracket A A] : Prop where
  lie_eq_mul_sub_mul (a b : A) : ⁅a, b⁆ = a * b - b * a

(probably with a better name) and then in statements where currently we assume [Ring A] and use docs#LieRing.ofAssociativeRing as a local instance, we would instead assume [Ring A] [LieRing A] [IsLieCommutator A].

One point I haven't decided would be whether to give a global docs#LieRing (and docs#LieAlgebra) instance on Module.End R M. I would certainly be useful and would mean that docs#LieModule.toEnd can still be a docs#LieHom
Aah, both are good suggestions!
HasCommutatorBracket?
